questions.question: Describe the composition of a business cycle as you would label it on a diagram, and define length and amplitude.
questions.expected_answer: A business cycle is the successive periods of expansion and contraction in real economic activity around a long-term growth trend. On the diagram, time runs on the horizontal axis and real GDP on the vertical; a gently rising straight line shows the trend, with a wave snaking around it. The four phases in order are the trough (the lowest point, where activity stops falling), the upswing or expansion (production, income, employment and spending rising), the peak (the highest point, where activity stops rising, often with capacity strained and prices accelerating) and the downswing or contraction (activity falling to the next trough). Peak and trough are the turning points. The length of the cycle is the time from one peak to the next peak (or trough to trough); the amplitude is the vertical distance between the trend line and a peak or trough, measuring the intensity of the cycle — the larger the amplitude, the stronger the shock and the longer its effects last.

questions.question: Contrast the exogenous and endogenous explanations of business cycles, naming the school associated with each and its policy conclusion, and list the four cycle types with their lengths and drivers.
questions.expected_answer: Exogenous explanations, associated with the monetarists, locate the causes outside the market system — weather, wars, oil shocks, pandemics and especially government policy mistakes such as erratic money supply growth. Markets are seen as stable and self-correcting, so the policy conclusion is stable, predictable, rules-based policy rather than intervention. Endogenous explanations, associated with the Keynesians, locate the causes inside the market system: sticky prices and wages, and swings in business confidence that feed on themselves through the multiplier and accelerator. Markets are seen as inherently unstable, so government must intervene to smooth the cycle. The four types: Kitchin cycles of roughly 3-5 years driven by inventories; Juglar cycles of 7-11 years driven by investment in machinery; Kuznets cycles of 15-20 years driven by building and construction; Kondratieff waves of 45-60 years driven by fundamental technological revolutions.

questions.question: Explain how monetary and fiscal policy are used to smooth the business cycle, and evaluate the forecasting toolkit of indicators, moving averages and extrapolation.
questions.expected_answer: In a downswing the SARB applies expansionary monetary policy — cutting the repo rate (to a record 3,5 percent in 2020), buying securities in open-market transactions and easing credit — while in an inflationary upswing it applies contractionary policy, raising the repo as in 2022-23 to defend the 3-6 percent inflation target. Fiscal policy works through the budget: expansionary policy raises spending and cuts taxes in a downswing, letting the multiplier amplify the injection; contractionary policy restrains spending in an overheating upswing. Automatic stabilisers — progressive tax and grants/UIF — dampen the cycle without new decisions. Both instruments act with lags and cannot fix supply-side constraints. For forecasting: leading indicators (new orders, building plans, share prices, confidence) turn before the economy; coincident indicators (retail sales, production) turn with it; lagging indicators (unemployment) turn after. Moving averages smooth noisy series to reveal direction; extrapolation projects the trend forward but assumes the future repeats the past, which fails at turning points — so indicators give direction, not dates or sizes.
